Intellectual property counsel.
A builder’s perspective.

I’m an intellectual property attorney and registered U.S. patent attorney. Before law, I built software. Today, I help businesses protect inventions and creative work, resolve IP disputes, and make sound decisions about technology.

Contact me at Kean Miller ↗ Professional biography ↗
Background

From software
to intellectual property.

At Duke, I studied computer science and psychology. The work that followed was practical: Java virtual machine performance at Motorola, streaming media at Blastro, and video-surveillance and business software at Model Software. Writing code meant working through architecture, databases, interfaces, and the details that determine whether a system does what its designer intended.

Tulane Law School gave me another set of systems to understand. My writing examined copyright and the First Amendment; my work on the Durationator put international copyright rules into executable form. Becoming a lawyer brought those interests together: understanding how something works, asking careful questions, and finding a useful way forward.

I’ve written code and HTML in Vim and worked with Linux systems and open-source software. My GitHub profile offers another look at that side of my work.

Working together

What I bring
to a matter.

The details matter. So does understanding what a client is trying to accomplish.

Explore representative matters ↗

Protection starts with understanding the work. My patent practice spans software, mechanical systems, and oil-and-gas technologies, from application preparation and prosecution to portfolio strategy. Firsthand development experience helps me work with inventors on the technical details behind a disclosure and its claims. Software patent prosecution is one part of that broader practice.

A dispute needs both detail and perspective. My experience includes patent litigation, PTAB proceedings, trademark enforcement and defense, copyright disputes, and trade secrets. Understanding the underlying technology or creative work helps me assess the issues and explain them clearly. My work also includes trademark protection and copyright ownership and enforcement.

An agreement should fit the actual project. For software contracts and technology licensing, that means working through scope, deliverables, code ownership, third-party components, open-source licenses, and ongoing responsibilities alongside the commercial terms.

The Durationator · Tulane Law School

Turning legal rules
into software.

Copyright law, expressed as executable logic.

At Tulane, I developed a general-purpose language, parser, and logic interpreter for the Durationator, software for analyzing copyright terms worldwide. The project required translating complicated legal rules into something a computer could evaluate.

Professor Elizabeth Townsend Gard discussed the challenges of developing the Durationator in her 2011 law review article. Justice Breyer cited pages 216–220 of her article in Golan v. Holder, 565 U.S. 302, 357 (2012) (Breyer, J., dissenting), when discussing the difficulty of determining copyright restoration under 17 U.S.C. § 104A.

Elizabeth Townsend Gard, In the Trenches with § 104A: An Evaluation of the Parties’ Arguments in Golan v. Holder as It Heads to the Supreme Court, 64 Vand. L. Rev. En Banc 199 (2011).

2009

A legal library, in a pocket.

In 2009, I developed and released the first Louisiana Civil Code app for iPhone. I also built an app for the Code of Civil Procedure—practical, searchable references for lawyers. Read the original iPhone J.D. review or explore the software projects.

Professional background

Teaching &
credentials.

Teaching trademark law through practice

From 2018 to 2021, I served as an Adjunct Professor at Tulane Law School, running the trademark section of its Intellectual Property Law Clinic. I taught students trademark law and supervised their work helping people apply for and obtain trademark registrations.

The clinic connected classroom study to the decisions and responsibilities of representing someone with a real legal need.

Selected Publications

While attending Tulane Law School, I published two works in the Tulane Journal of Technology & Intellectual Property examining the intersection of copyright law and the First Amendment. Both addressed constitutional issues surrounding copyright protection that were then working their way through the federal courts.

Law review publications

  1. The Trouble with Traditions: The Split over Eldred’s Traditional Contours Guidelines, How They Might Be Applied, and Why They Ultimately Fail

    J. Matthew Miller III, 11 Tul. J. Tech. & Intell. Prop. 91 (2008).

    Examines the traditional contours framework from Eldred v. Ashcroft, its differing application by the federal courts, and its shortcomings as a guide to First Amendment scrutiny of copyright law.

  2. Golan v. Gonzales: How Copyright Restoration Alters the Ordinary Copyright Sequence and Invites First Amendment Review

    J. Matthew Miller III, 10 Tul. J. Tech. & Intell. Prop. 353 (2007).

    Analyzes the Tenth Circuit’s decision on restoring copyright protection to foreign works previously in the public domain and the resulting First Amendment questions.

Computer science conference abstract

My interest in emerging technology goes back to my undergraduate years. In 1998, I coauthored a conference abstract on the use of virtual reality in education, published in the proceedings of ACM SIGGRAPH ’98.

  1. Virtual Reality in Education: Irish and American Students Meet on the Virtual Frontier

    Casey D. Charvet, J. Matthew Miller III, and Jonah H. Peretti. (1998). In ACM SIGGRAPH ’98 Conference Abstracts and Applications, p. 60. Association for Computing Machinery (ACM). DOI: 10.1145/280953.281002.
